Thank you for submitting your article "Single-cell transcriptome analysis of neural crest migration reveals signatures of invasion and molecular transitions" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Marianne Bronner as the Senior and Reviewing Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission. I have attached the full reviews of both reviewers which are highly concordant. While they feel that the data are valuable as a Tools and Resource paper, both reviewers felt that the way the manuscript was presented was confusing and that it would be important to rewrite the manuscript in a manner that doesn't over interpret the results. I think that you would be able to do this with textual revisions alone but would urge you to spend particular care on addressing the points raised in the full reviews, as both reviewers commented that they felt you had not addressed their earlier concerns and were trying too hard to put your conclusions in a positive light rather than addressing the caveats of the single cell RNA-seq analysis and the difficulties of linking this to in vivo expression analysis and function.

Given the history of this manuscript, this must be your last opportunity to produce an acceptable version.

Essential revisions:

1) The authors should aim to provide a clear, and accurate description of their findings. These in vivo findings need to be spelled clearly: These genes were identified by scRNAseq and bioinformatics (through a stringent protocol with harsh significance in mind), as specific to the expected Trailblazer at the narrow front edge of the migratory front, however, they do not seem to appear restricted in that fashion in vivo, and insteada) None of the 13 genes tested so far (which include some of the top candidates) are expressed in all of, or the majority of the cells at the front edge.b) some may appear in a few or some but not in all of the cells (~30% or 1/3?) of the (narrow) front migratory edge.c) some of the genes may display salt and pepper patterns which may include strong expression in a few cells in the narrow front edge and similarly strong signal in some cells in the beginning or middle portions of the stream (not at the front edge of migration).d) Some of the genes where not found at the front edge at all, and instead appear to be expressed more strongly at various positions within the migratory stream.

2) The authors should provide a revised version of the so called "complex profile/signature of expression for a Trailblazer" If the genes are not specifically expressed in all of them, or the majority, and if these genes may be expressed in the stream, then what is the so called complex signature of the trail blazer? (Not to mention its relevance…) The authors could offer some useful insights regarding the limitations or caveats of the scRNAseq at the current time/or in these complex settings. Perhaps cumulative RNA vs. freshly made RNA.

3) The novel RNAscope data shows heterogeneous expression of genes that are part of the "Trailblazer signature". While this reviewer finds that a thorough transcriptomic characterization of single RNA cells may be a useful resource for the community, the results of the in vivo analysis require further clarification.

4) Upon presenting the expanded RNAscope analysis, the authors conclude that "the combination of fluorescence in situ hybridization with IHC and tissue clearing allowed the confirmation of a small subset of the Trailblazer transcriptional signature". This statement seems to imply that heterogeneous expression is sufficient to validate transcripts as being part of the Trailblazer signature. According the Introduction of the manuscript such genes should be expressed by cells "narrowly confined by the migratory front". This discrepancy needs to be addressed or the reader will not be able to link the transcriptomic data with the in vivo expression analysis.

Reviewer #1:

The Authors previously used cell sorting and q-RT-PCR to identify a unique molecular signature of 16 out of 96 genes that was stable and consistent in cranial neural crest cells narrowly confined to the most invasive front of the migratory stream that we termed 'Trailblazers' (McLennan et al., 2015). In this manuscript, they have further scrutinized the expression profile of individual cells to address molecular changes and singularities that could help us better understand the behavior of migrating cells, specifically those at the fore front of the migration. The appealing idea being that these front runners might be endowed with unique capabilities to determine direction, remove ECM, perhaps even push other cells to the side, open a path, and lay the road and or instructions for follower cells.

There is a lot of value in this hard and fine work. They had accomplished a technically challenging task addressing the expression profiles of migrating neural crest cells. They provide significant information regarding the differences between in vitro cultured and in vivo migrating neural crest cells. They confirm some of the genes they previously identified as enriched in the "Trailblazer" cells using a single cell RNA seq approach. Yet the outcome of this huge endeavor in its present format, is misleading. As presented by the authors, one would assume that they have identified a unique "expression signature" of Trailblazer cells, which migrate at the front edge of the migratory stream in chick embryos, which they define as "narrowly confined by the migratory front". The implication being that a few genes would be expressed in a specific pattern associated with the migratory front edge. Does this mean a strong expression of a few genes consistent at the front edge? This argument is made throughout the paper in multiple places. But they do not provide the evidence necessary to grant such claim, and should be corrected throughout.

Key to these arguments would be a clear, measurable, objective definition of the front edge. In terms of its distance from the dorsal neural tube or departure point, truly the edge, near the edge, 2, 3 5 cells behind the apparent edge? And then the width or range of the front edge, all the cells visible at the edge? Some angle or curvature to restrict it? And what is the volume of the front edge? The use of ill-defined, subjective terms provides ample room for misinterpretation and confusion.

If we were to think of our arm and hand as a migratory stream departing from our trunk, what could be considered as the Trailblazers, the nails? The tip of the thumb? Or the index fingers only, the distal, middle or proximal portions of some or all of the phalanges? Would it be enough to look at the back of the hand/dorsal portion of the phalanges, or the palm portion/ ventral, or the middle? etc…

While performing the transcriptomic portion of the work, a lot of effort was placed to define and collect cells from specific regions of the stream to be analyzed. Yet upon validation of expression in embryos, a much laxer approach is taken and confusion ensues.

The heading of one of the Results sections reads: "Trailblazer cells are identified by an ensemble of genes", and after presenting the results in cryptic and limited format, concludes: "Thus, the combination of fluorescence in situ hybridization with IHC and tissue clearing allowed the confirmation of a small subset of the Trailblazer transcriptional signature." Yet the expression of the genes here presented is not restricted or biased to the front edge.

The authors perform single cell transcriptomics and come up with a selected list of genes thought to decipher the molecular signature of the "Trailblazer" cell. They try to corroborate their thorough and delicate transcriptomics and bioinformatics work via two assessments. The first one consisting of expression analysis, and the second on Morpholino mediated knockdown. The knockdown provided minimal effects at best and thus could not confirm the tenants of a "relevant" trailblazer expression. Perhaps combinatorial approaches could reveal function, but at this point no more evidence is provided.

To demonstrate expression profile associated with Trailblazer character, the authors performed a nice combination of immunofluorescence to identify all the migratory NC via HNK1, combined with quantifiable in situ hybridization analysis, "RNAscope". The criteria provided to select genes to prove and validate the trailblazer character states:

1) genes with enriched expression in Trailblazer cells;

2) high percentage of single Trailblazer cells in which the gene was detected and;

3) high level at which the gene was expressed by the Trailblazer cells.

(The genes tested are PKP2, DESMIN, KAZALD1, TESCALCIN, TROPONIN, ANEXIN, BAMBI, GLYPICAN3, DESMOPLAKIN, BDNF, TFPI2, NEXILIN, CDH5).

In no case, a unique pattern is presented that strictly labels with the highest signal the expected trailblazer cells at the front edge of the migratory stream defined as "narrowly confined by the migratory front". Instead, in the best cases for their argument (PKP2, and KAZALD1), expression seem to appear strong or strongest in a few of the visible trailblazer cells. These genes do not appear consistently in their strongest expression profile at the front edge, in all the trailblazers. Some Trailblazer cells clearly do not express these genes and or express them weaker than follower cells. And in multiple cases stream or follower cells display a wide range of expression levels varying from the strongest to no expression. And one has to wonder what is the depth of the image presented? Does this represent the whole edge, or would one imagine 3 similar projections to cover the volume of the front edge? If so, what is the number of cells at the front edge that strongly express the interrogated marker? Further, when they analyze the expression relative to neighbors, the effort is limited to very few cells, when the same arguments made for distance to the edge, width and depth should apply.

This is even more clear when analyzing the other 11 genes they present. Desmin, and Troponin1, display 1 and 2 cells respectively, with the strongest expression (red) far behind the expected Trailblazers (are not at the very front) and instead are behind multiple cells with 2/3 or 1/2 as much expression. And unfortunately, the evidence provided for their analysis of the additional other 8 genes, does not support their case either, and actually are not a better example of what one would have expected for a trailblazer profile of expression.

Importantly, for some undisclosed reason, they do not include the same targets on expression and function (only 3 of the 9 targets assessed via Morpholinos are also tested amongst the 13 targets used for expression analysis with RNSAscope).

Given the lack of evidence of relevant role for the genes tested, and that no signature is confirmed by expression in the embryo, the current version would be a misleading tool or resource.

The authors should provide a revised version of the so called "complex profile/signature of expression for a Trailblazer" If the genes are not specifically expressed in all of them, or the majority, and if these genes may be expressed in the stream, then what is the so called complex signature of the trail blazer? This revised version of the manuscript by Morrisson and colleagues on scRNA-seq analysis of neural crest cells includes an expanded RNAscope analysis of putative Trailblazer genes. Reviews of the previous versions of the manuscript emphasize the need for further in vivo validation of the transcriptomic datasets. results.result: This study performed the first single-cell transcriptome analysis of cranial neural crest cell migration at three progressive developmental stages (HHSt11, 13, 15) in chick, analyzing 469 cells from spatially distinct subregions (Front, Lead, Trail) of the migratory stream. The analysis identified and established hierarchical relationships between cell position- and time-specific transcriptional profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10, C23-C27, C147-C148 collectively describe the experimental design and scope of the study. The methodology is clearly described with specific numbers of cells (469), developmental stages (HHSt11, 13, 15), and spatial subdivisions (Front 5%, Lead 25%, Trail 70%). Quality control metrics and hierarchical clustering analyses support the identification of distinct transcriptional profiles.

results.result: Bulk RNA-seq analysis of neural crest cells from the invasive front versus the remainder of the stream at HHSt13 and HHSt15 revealed statistically significant differences in gene expression, with 23 genes consistently enriched and 19 genes consistently reduced in the front across both stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C22 describe bulk RNA-seq experiments with appropriate biological replicates (n=3), quality control (C16), and statistical validation (C17). The identification of 23 up-regulated and 19 down-regulated genes (C19-C20) is supported by hierarchical clustering and Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1. The validation of specific genes from previous RT-qPCR studies (C21-C22) strengthens the findings.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis revealed that spatial location within the stream and temporal progression along the migratory pathway are primary determinants of gene expression, with distinct molecular signatures for each subpopulation (Front, Lead, Trail) but also substantial heterogeneity within subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29, C38-C43 are supported by hierarchical clustering (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 3) and Pearson correlation analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The identification of gene subsets that increase/decrease with developmental stage (C38), are uniquely expressed in specific subpopulations (C39), or correlate with spatial position (C40) is demonstrated through heatmap analysis. The observation of heterogeneity (C41-C42) is appropriately documented.

results.result: In vitro neural crest cell transcriptional profiles are prominently distinct from all in vivo profiles, with 806 genes down-regulated and 312 genes up-regulated in vitro compared to in vivo, suggesting that the in vivo embryonic microenvironment critically influences neural crest cell gene expression and biological processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37, C141-C144 are well-supported by Pearson correlation matrix (Figure 2C), PCA analysis (Figure 2D), and GO term analysis (Figure 2E). The identification of 806 down-regulated and 312 up-regulated genes (C34-C35) is documented with specific examples. The lack of GO term enrichment for up-regulated genes (C36) is appropriately noted. The conclusion about microenvironmental influence (C37, C144) is supported by comparison with previous RT-qPCR data (C142-C143).

results.result: Hierarchical clustering and PCA analysis of invasive front cells identified five distinct subpopulations: two clusters at HHSt11 (Cluster1 and Cluster2), Lead-like cells at HHSt13 and HHSt15, and a distinct Trailblazer cluster containing cells from all three developmental stages with minimal overlap with other subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are supported by hierarchical clustering (Figure 4A), Pearson correlation matrix (Figure 4B), and PCA analysis (Figure 4C). The identification of five distinct subpopulations is clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical methods. The Trailblazer cluster shows consistent separation from other subpopulations across all three developmental stages, representing a more comprehensive analysis than previous RT-qPCR work (C49).

results.result: The Trailblazer transcriptional signature is characterized by 964 up-regulated and 406 down-regulated genes, with Trailblazer cells representing approximately 8% of cells at HHSt11, 49% of invasive front cells at HHSt13 (~12 cells), and 32% at HHSt15 (~13 cells), and mostly confined to the invasive front with fewer than 10% of cells in other stream regions showing overlapping expression profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C50-C60 are supported by volcano plot analysis (Figure 5A), comparison with bulk RNA-seq (C52-C53 showing 79% and 37% overlap), and PCA analysis (Figure 5C). The quantification of Trailblazer cell proportions (C56-C58) is based on clustering analysis. The spatial restriction to the invasive front (C59-C60) is demonstrated by PCA showing <10% overlap with Lead and Trail cells. The approximate number of 900 genes (C2) is consistent with 964 up-regulated genes (C50).

results.result: Pathway analysis of the Trailblazer signature revealed that 81% of differentially expressed genes in known pathways were increased, including genes associated with WNT/Beta Catenin, EMT, integrin, and BMP signaling, with increased expression of VEGF receptors 1, 2, and 3 and neuropilin-1 (NRP1), strengthening support for VEGF chemoattraction in neural crest migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64, C127-C129 are supported by pathway enrichment analysis (Figure 5D) using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. The 81% increase versus 19% decrease (C61) is clearly documented. The identification of specific pathways (C62) and VEGF signaling components (C63) is consistent with previous functional studies showing that neuropilin-1 knockdown prevents branchial arch invasion (C128). The connection to prior work (C127-C129) appropriately contextualizes the findings.

results.result: Thirty-seven genes associated with axonal guidance signaling are expressed at significantly higher levels in Trailblazers, including members of the BMP, EPH, MMP, and WNT families, with only 7 of 26 axonal guidance genes previously examined in neural crest migration, suggesting shared molecular features between neural crest invasion and axonal growth cone guidance.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C130-C134 are supported by pathway analysis (Figure 5D) and literature review. The identification of 37 axonal guidance genes (C64) is documented, and the observation that only 7 of 26 have been previously studied in neural crest (C133) is supported by citations. The connection to neurovascular patterning (C131) and the suggestion of shared molecular features (C132) are appropriately framed as emerging evidence and inference. The speculation about future research (C134) is reasonable but does not affect the core finding.

results.result: Comparison of scRNA-seq Trailblazer signature with the previous 16-gene RT-qPCR signature revealed that four genes (AQP1, BAMBI, CTNNB1, PKP2) were enriched in both analyses, with differences explained by methodological variances (RT-qPCR sensitivity versus scRNA-seq comprehensiveness) and inclusion of HHSt11 cells in the scRNA-seq analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69, C135-C138 appropriately compare the current scRNA-seq results with previous RT-qPCR work (McLennan et al., 2015). The identification of four overlapping genes (C65) is shown in Figure 5E. The explanation for partial overlap (C135-C138) is reasonable, noting differences in cell selection criteria (C136), methodological sensitivity (C137), and inclusion of additional developmental stages (C138). The analysis acknowledges both validation and refinement of previous findings.

results.result: RNAscope expression analysis of 13 Trailblazer genes revealed that none were expressed in all or the majority of cells at the invasive front, with some genes showing heterogeneous expression (~30% of front cells), salt and pepper patterns including expression in middle/back portions of the stream, or expression outside the invasive front, with potential technical limitations including differences in sensitivity between scRNA-seq and RNAscope and difficulty visualizing low numbers of Trailblazer cells in 3D.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C70-C75, C118-C120 describe RNAscope validation results that are inconsistent with the scRNA-seq Trailblazer signature. While the RNAscope data (Figure 6A-M) are clearly presented, the lack of expression restriction to the invasive front (C70-C75) contradicts the scRNA-seq findings (C59-C60). The authors appropriately acknowledge potential technical limitations (C118-C120), including sensitivity differences and visualization challenges, but these explanations are speculative. The inconsistency between transcriptomic and spatial expression data creates uncertainty about the spatial restriction of the Trailblazer signature.

results.result: Morpholino knockdown of three Trailblazer genes (WNT5B, PKP2, EDN1) showed significant but modest reductions in neural crest cell distance migrated (21%, 13%, and >13% respectively), with validation by RT-PCR for splice-blocking morpholinos, while overall stream migration remained >90% of normal distance, suggesting cell-autonomous effects with wildtype cells compensating for knockdown cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 describe morpholino knockdown experiments with appropriate controls and statistical analysis (p-values provided). The modest effects (C76-C78) are clearly documented in Figure 6N-Q, with validation by RT-PCR (C81-C82, Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The observation that overall stream migration is minimally affected (C83, Figure 6—figure supplement 3) supports the interpretation of cell-autonomous effects with compensation by wildtype cells (C84). The lack of correlation between expression level and functional effect (C80) is appropriately noted. However, the modest effects and compensation by wildtype cells limit the strength of functional conclusions.

results.result: Neural crest cells at HHSt11 cluster into two distinct subpopulations: Cluster1 enriched for neural plate border genes (WNT3, WNT3A, WNT7B, WNT8B, ZIC1, ZIC3, MSX1, CDH6, EphA7, CDH2, and novel transcription factor PAX6) with increased signaling pathway genes (59%), and Cluster2 enriched for later specification/EMT/migration genes (PAX3, TFAP2B, SOX8, FHL2) with decreased signaling pathway genes (1%), suggesting a rapid molecular switch from EMT to directed migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C99, C139-C140 are supported by volcano plots (Figure 7A-B), GO term analysis (Figure 7C-D), and pathway enrichment analysis (Figure 7E-F). The identification of Cluster1 genes associated with neural plate border (C85-C86) is consistent with previous work (Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015). The discovery of PAX6 enrichment (C88) represents a novel finding. The Cluster2 signature (C89-C92) shows appropriate EMT/migration genes. The dramatic difference in pathway gene expression (C95-C99) and minimal overlap between clusters (C140) support the interpretation of a rapid molecular switch (C139-C140) rather than gradual transition.

results.result: Lead and Trail subpopulations show distinct transcriptional signatures with relatively small numbers of differentially expressed genes: at HHSt13, Trail had 45 enriched and 151 reduced genes while Lead had 26 enriched and 35 reduced genes; at HHSt15, Trail had 174 enriched and 132 reduced genes while Lead had 77 enriched and 138 reduced genes, with pathway analysis revealing reduced expression of developmental signaling pathways including VEGF, actin cytoskeleton, integrin, axonal guidance, and ephrin receptor signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C108 are supported by volcano plots (Figure 8A-B, D-E) and pathway enrichment analysis (Figure 8C, F). The identification of specific numbers of differentially expressed genes (C100, C104, C107) is documented with examples (C101-C102, C105). The pathway analysis (C103, C106, C108) shows consistent reduction of developmental signaling pathways. However, the relatively small numbers of differentially expressed genes and high heterogeneity within these large subpopulations (noted in text) suggest these signatures are less robust than the Trailblazer signature.

results.result: Four main features contribute to cranial neural crest migration: (1) majority of invasive front cells change gene expression during migration while a small Trailblazer subpopulation maintains a conserved signature; (2) newly exited cells cluster into two subpopulations indicating rapid EMT to migration transition; (3) Lead cells cluster with non-Trailblazer invasive front cells; (4) Trail cells cluster with newly exited and in vitro cells, which have distinct profiles from all in vivo populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 represent summary statements of the main findings in the discussion. These conclusions are supported by the collective evidence from hierarchical clustering, PCA analysis, and differential expression analyses described in previous result groups. The four features appropriately synthesize the spatial and temporal transcriptional dynamics observed throughout the study. These are interpretive conclusions that integrate multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: The number of genes up-regulated in the invasive front was consistent between HHSt13 (61 genes) and HHSt15 (55 genes) with 23 genes overlapping, while down-regulated genes showed a nearly 4-fold difference (255 genes at HHSt13 versus 36 at HHSt15) with 19 genes overlapping, confirming rapid molecular changes as cells encounter the branchial arch microenvironment, with the 42 overlapping genes representing a conserved molecular signature.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 provide quantitative analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from Figure 1. The numbers are clearly documented in the heatmaps and Venn diagrams. The interpretation of the 4-fold difference in down-regulated genes (C116) as indicating rapid microenvironmental response is reasonable. The identification of 42 conserved genes (C117) across both stages is appropriately characterized as a stable signature during the transition.

results.result: Several Trailblazer genes (AQP1, BAMBI, CTNNB1, PKP2, Tescalcin, WNT5B) have been implicated in human cancer cell invasion and metastasis, suggesting these genes may have critical functional roles in both neural crest migration and cancer aggressiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C126 connect Trailblazer genes to cancer biology through literature citations. The specific examples (BAMBI in colorectal/osteosarcoma C122, PKP2 in glioma/bladder cancer C123, Tescalcin in colorectal cancer C124, WNT5B in multiple cancers C125) are supported by appropriate citations. The suggestion that these genes may be part of a broader molecular signature in cancer aggressiveness (C126) is appropriately framed as inference and speculation. This represents valid contextualization of the findings within broader biological significance.

results.result: This study addresses the challenge of identifying distinct transcriptional signatures in dynamic cell populations during migration by providing the first comprehensive single-cell transcriptome analysis of neural crest migration across three developmental stages, revealing hierarchical relationships between cell position- and time-specific profiles and providing insights into molecular patterns underlying directed, collective cell migration with implications for other migratory phenomena.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 represent summary statements about the study's significance and contribution. The claim of being the first comprehensive single-cell analysis of neural crest migration (C147) is supported by the scope of the work (469 cells, three stages, multiple spatial positions). The identification of hierarchical relationships (C148) is demonstrated through multiple analytical approaches. The broader significance (C149) is appropriately framed. These are valid summary statements supported by the collective evidence.

results.result: The study employed standard methods for chick embryo manipulation, cell labeling, tissue dissection, FACS isolation, bulk and single-cell RNA-seq library preparation using SMART-seq v4, sequencing on HiSeq 2500, computational analysis using Tophat, edgeR, ClusterProfiler, and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis, and RNAscope combined with immunohistochemistry for spatial expression validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C176 describe the experimental and computational methods. The methods are clearly described with appropriate detail including specific reagents, instruments, software versions, and parameters. The choice of SMART-seq v4 is justified for detecting maximum genes per cell (C164). Quality control metrics are provided (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The computational pipeline is standard and appropriate. The RNAscope protocol is adapted from published methods (C174). These methodological claims are well-supported and reproducible.

results.result: Background knowledge claims establish that neural crest cells undergo EMT to exit the dorsal neural tube, cranial neural crest cells travel in multicellular streams beneath the surface ectoderm, the chick embryo is well-suited for studying neural crest migration with optimized techniques, and previous work identified a 16-gene Trailblazer signature with functional evidence from transcription factor overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C9 represent established knowledge and previous work that provides context for the current study. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature (Morrison et al., 2012, 2015; McLennan et al., 2015). The background information is accurate and relevant to the study design and interpretation.
